en: Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Master Xishan, composed by the Bhikṣu Huizhen.
The Bhikṣu Huizhen is about to publish the recorded sayings of Master Xishan Liang. As he is an old friend of mine from thirty years ago, he came to the hermitage at Fiquan and requested a preface.
I washed my pen and presented this to him, saying: [The text continues with the preface itself.]
For forty-eight years deceiving later generations, He has barely opened his foul mouth to slander the ancestral school.
Now he further carves out idle topics for promotion; Striking the water, he seeks the traces of the staff as before.
Written on the first day of the New Year in the third year of Chunyou by the Woodcutter of Tianmu (Wenli) at the Merit Hall of Lord Li.
While in seclusion at the temple, I ascended the five peaks in succession to request Wuzhun’s colophon for this work. Having received it, I could not decline;
I do so hoping that others will not brush aside my idle words as if they were those of a mere messenger.
The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Xishan Liang,
Compiled by Attendant Juexin: The Record of the Sayings of Venerable Xishan while Residing at the Qingshen Chan Monastery in Jiankang Prefecture.
In the fourth year of the Jiading era, the Master ascended the hall and said:
"He raised the case of Zen Master Sansheng, who said: 'When I meet a person, I come forth; when I come forth, I do not act for the sake of others.
Xinghua said: 'When I meet a person, I do not come forth; when I come forth, I immediately act for the sake of others. Both Sansheng and Xinghua each brought forth one leg."

[The Master] said, "Hand! You wish to uphold the Linji school’s style, yet you do not realize that the Linji school’s style has already been swept away to its very foundations by those two great elders.
Now, as Layman Liang enters the world [to teach], how will it ultimately be?
Fortunately, we are guests in an era of peace and no affairs; why must we brandish weapons when we meet? Even so, this too is what Xuefeng would have said."
Ascending the hall, he said: "A single leaf falls and autumn comes to all under heaven; how many can discern its origin here? The patch-robed monk laughs heartily from a cold place;
Nan Yue and Tiantai are on the tip of his staff."
Ascending the hall, the Master raised the following case: Nan-yuan asked a monk, "What is your name? The monk replied, "Pu-chan. Nan-yuan said, "What if you suddenly encounter a piece of excrement?

The monk said, "I do not know [how to respond]. Nan-yuan then struck him. The Master said: "Two pieces of excrement, joined into one mass—smelling to the heavens and scorching the earth, who could bear to sniff it?
For a thousand ages, this has served as a topic for the monastic community."
Ascending the hall: This morning is the fifteenth day of the eleventh month. Time flies like an arrow; the year draws to a close. How should one practice Chan and study the Way?
One must strictly avoid sitting and waiting for a rabbit at a stump. If you are a true cub of the golden-haired lion, you will turn back with a single leap, leaving no room for hesitation.
No room for hesitation! You would startle even the white-browed tiger of the Southern Mountain.
Ascending the hall: When two nations wage war and the myriad people flee in all directions, it reaches the point where the front porches and rear galleries of the mosque are occupied all at once;
oxen are tied in the Buddha Hall and horses are tied in the Sangha Hall, with no space left for defecating or urinating.
In such a state, even those with iron brows and copper heads would be terrified; yet only the Old Man Śākyamuni remains joyful.
Joyful joy! Coming and going upon a heap of excrement, emitting light and shaking the earth—do you all see it?
If you can see it, then night after night you embrace the Buddha in sleep, and morning after morning you rise together with him. If this is not yet so, do not say you are without fault.
[He] struck the meditation seat and descended from it.
Ascending the hall: This morning is the middle of the third month; the myriad flowers bloom in full splendor. The meaning of the Patriarchs is exceedingly clear;
why not look with your own eyes? Look, look! Suddenly the flowers fall and the branches are bare; once again they are blown by the wind into a different tune.
Ascending the hall, the Master raised an ancient case: A monk asked Baoci, "When emotion arises, wisdom is obstructed; when thought changes, the essence becomes distinct.
Before emotion has arisen, what then? Baoci replied, "Obstructed. The Master said, "The point where this monk asked was free from all confusion; he immediately took it up and handed it over to him."
A single red dot upon a tender green branch; such moving springtime requires no more.
Ascending the hall at the end of the summer retreat: The ninety-day restriction of the feet is fulfilled this day. The lacquer bucket is overturned—a person of joyous ease.
Do not take offense at my chest-beating and boasting of solitary mastery; It is simply because I have spent the summer in the realm of True Purity.

Ascending the hall, [Dahui] raised the case: Zhaozhou asked Nanquan, "Where does a person who 'knows' go? Nanquan said, "He goes to become a water buffalo at a lay patron's house. Zhaozhou said, "Thank you for your answer, Master. Nanquan said, "Last night at the third watch, the moon shone through the window.

Yunfeng said, "If Nanquan had not had these subsequent words, he would have been captured and taken to Cai Prefecture. Dahui said: "Nanquan was like a man who, having already reached the city walls, suddenly turns back and tries to scale the ramparts. He was so clumsy that he ended up breaking his own neck. Zhaozhou was like a man who, having already entered the city, suddenly turns back and tries to scale the ramparts from the outside. He was so clumsy that he ended up breaking his own neck.

As for Yunfeng, he was like a man who, having already entered the city, suddenly turns back and tries to scale the ramparts from the inside. He was so clumsy that he ended up breaking his own neck. If Nanquan had not had these subsequent words, he would have been captured and taken to Cai Prefecture. But even if he had not had these subsequent words, he still would have been captured and taken to Cai Prefecture. Why? Because there is no place to hide."
The Master’s Patriarch said, "The old man Yunfeng lost one eye. He did not realize that it was precisely because of his later words that he shattered Caizhou on the spot.
The Master said, "When walking reaches the end of the water, sit and watch the clouds arise."
Opening the furnace, he ascends the hall. He cites the Venerable Zhaozhou, who said: "At the head of the brazier, there is a saying that has neither guest nor host.
In my thirty years in the South, not a single person has ever brought it up. The Master says: "Old Zhaozhou was far too insatiable.
Today, as we open the furnace, I, Qingzhen, cannot help but add a head atop a head. He recites the saying of "no guest, no host" once more.
Having bestowed the alms upon the great assembly, he descended from his seat and ascended the hall.

He spoke of the boundless transgressions of practicing Chan, saying that such things are merely ready-made wares for sale; it is a pity that people turn their backs on awakening and unite with the dust of the senses.
Enduring hunger by the side of a rice basket.
Compiled by Attendant Zhìqīng from the *Recorded Sayings* of Wéishān Hóngshòu,
who resided at Língyǐn Chan Monastery in Qìngyuán Prefecture.

Pointing to the three gates, he tramples the paths of a thousand differences; the gateways that reach the heavens stand wide open. Lifting his head, the sky is vast and empty; beneath his feet, wind and thunder arise.
[He] takes up the notice.
To issue commands to both the holy and the ordinary, one must rely upon this very thing. But tell me, from where does this come?
Do you know? Stop up your ears and listen clearly!
Ascending the hall, he said: "The heart of this eighty-year-old old woman has long since turned to ash; she forces her face with rouge and applies vermilion.

Knowing herself to be decrepit and devoid of shame, when the mood strikes, why not dance once more? (Question and answer not recorded. "I, the Mountain Man, have now received a warrant from the Prefectural Office."
To cause the abbot to perform rites for the state, this morning he entered the monastery and ascended the hall;
beyond offering prayers for the Emperor’s long life, what else is there to discuss? If you wish to speak of rules and regulations, they follow one wherever one goes. If you wish to speak of Chan...

The Way. It kills people by leaving them stranded. After all, how is it? "When the waves of the four seas are calm, the dragon sleeps soundly; when the clouds of the nine heavens are still, the crane soars high.
When Baoshou opened the hall, Sansheng pushed forward a monk. "Giving a ladder to a thief," Baoshou then struck him. This was his command.
"Not acting in vain. The Three Sages said, "To act for others in such a manner not only blinds this monk’s eyes, but will blind the eyes of the entire city of Zhenzhou.
For the sake of the assembly, Baoshou threw down his staff and returned to his quarters. Does the assembly understand?
"Returning after a night of drunkenness under the bright moon, the music leads one into the painted hall."
Ascending the hall on the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month, he simply went about like this—already adding frost to snow.

How much more so when he speaks further of "seeing the morning star and attaining perfect enlightenment"? Such talk obscures the descendants of the Patriarchs. If Lingyin had seen him at that time, he would have simply said:
"Change the basin! Change the basin!"
Ascending the hall, he said: "Willows are green, flowers are red, and spring birds sing. Clearly, I declare the ancestral intent for you to know.
If you can realize the essential point directly within this, you have already fallen into my second device."
Ascending the hall at the commencement of the summer retreat. At the beginning of the *an-gu* (summer retreat), it is named "prohibiting the feet.

The meaning of "prohibiting the feet" lies in advancing on the Path and protecting living beings. But for us monks, what living being is there to protect? What Path is there to advance upon? Spit! Spit!
Spitting upon the face of Old Śākyamuni; taking a single step, he tramples the backbone of Old Śākyamuni.
O Great Assembly! When the Patriarch Baizhang speaks thus, it is very much like pressing one's eyes and seeing flowers. Under the gate of Lingyin—

Before Śākyamuni there was none; after Maitreya there shall be none. Speaking of the profound establishment and dissolution of the retreat, the long and short periods—throughout the twelve hours, in every place and at every moment—it is like a long sword leaning against the heavens: who would dare look directly upon it with their own eyes?
Do you all understand? (After a long silence) Even the single word "understand" is not necessary.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The matter of studying the Way is beyond all deliberation; quickly fix your eyes and swiftly take it up.
Everywhere is nothing but the land of peace and joy. A-he-he! How joyful! Even ten thousand taels of gold could not buy such a thing. Nevertheless, for now, let us eat our barley rice."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the following case: Yunmen asked Dongshan, "Where have you recently come from? Dongshan said, "From Chadu. Yunmen asked, "Where did you spend the summer?
Dongshan said, "At Baoci in Hunan. Yunmen asked, "When did you leave there? Dongshan said, "The twenty-fifth of the eighth month. Yunmen said, "I grant you three blows of the staff.
On the following day, Dongshan went to the abbot’s quarters to inquire after him, saying, "Yesterday..."
[The Master] said, "I have recently received the staff from Master Mung. I do not yet know where my fault lies. Mun said, "You rice-bag!
You go off to Jiangxi and Hunan acting just like this! The Master said, "Fierce winds and heavy rains crash with thunder; the entire courtyard shakes and the flowers fall in disarray.
Red and white petals are already strewn everywhere—why trouble yourself, rice-bag, to pick them up again?"
Ascending the hall, he said: "The golden wind rises and the tree leaves fall; the true body is revealed, majestic and agile. I inform you: grasp this quickly!
If you turn your head and twist your brain to try and deliberate, you will mistake a colander for a wooden ladle."
When Great Master Zhen visited [Master] Shangtang, he recounted the story of Jishi visiting Juzhi. Jishi did not remove his bamboo hat. Juzhi said, "Take it off.
Jishi replied, "If you can say something, then I will take it off. Juzhi was speechless. Jishi then departed. Juzhi called out, "Wait a moment!

Jishi replied, "If you can say something, then I will stay. Juzhi again was speechless. The Master said, "Setting aside the fact that he was speechless, Jishi was simply playing with cleverness and ending up clumsy."
The Great Master has come to visit us today; there is simply nothing that can be done about it. From this moment on, he stands a head above all ancients.
Let those with the true eye discern this for themselves.
Ascending the hall, he raised the example of Master Wuzu Yan showing his disciples: "It is like an ox passing through a window frame;
its two legs and four hooves have all passed through, yet why is it that the tail remains stuck? To this I say: 'Gu-gua!
Let him be filled with shame upon his own face."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the case of Elder Ming chasing Layman Lu to the summit of Mount Dayu. Seeing that he did not act upon his sense of righteousness, how could there be any valor?
Lu then cast his robe and bowl onto a rock, saying, "This robe represents the seal of faith; can it be contested by force?"

To withdraw oneself and yield to others is something that occurs but once in ten thousand cases. When Layman Ming raised this point, [Lu] remained as immovable as a mountain and said, "I have come for the sake of the Dharma, not for the sake of robes.

He earnestly requested instruction. As the words emerged from the prisoner's mouth, Lu said, "Neither thinking of good nor thinking of evil—what is the original face of Layman Ming? With a sword held at his head, he cut him through. Layman Ming...
To grant thirty blows for sitting and attaining great enlightenment under these words—after all, what was the place of awakening for Elder Ming?
He swept away the magnificent peaks of Mount Hua reaching to the heavens; he unleashed the Yellow River, pure to its very depths.
Verse: The plantain tree, the staff—do you have a staff, or do you not?
If you have a staff, give it back; if you have no staff, snatch it away! How many can truly overturn heaven and earth?
I know. The oriole’s song does not reside upon the flowering branches.

For how many years has Lingyun seen peach blossoms and wandered through lakes and seas without shame? Upon seeing the peach blossoms, he nodded his head himself—how laughable that those looking on still have eyes [to see].
It is hot! They come to join the ranks and display their flair.
When Zhaozhou examined the old woman, he surely heard her when she was hungry, and he surely heard her when she was full. While the old woman was at Mount Tai, Zhaozhou thoroughly investigated her.
The Snow Lion is a single color, its entire body white; naturally, it is free from even a speck of dust. It stands upon the ancient path; though it does not roar, it still startles people.
The Prefectural Magistrate Huang of Jiankang invited him to reside at Qingzhen Monastery, but he declined with a verse.
Having reached the very marrow of one's bones through poverty, one never tires of being poor. Reclining at ease amidst the white clouds, one eats a single bowl of mixed rice for sustenance;
beyond this, there is nothing else capable of sustaining the ancestral wind.
Lamenting how Duan’an,
for no reason, twisted the crooked to make it straight and plainly changed people’s eyes; now that he has departed with his single sandal,
let us rejoice that all under heaven is at peace.
The wicker mat and bamboo screen are fused into one, as still and clear as water. The wind cannot stir them, yet a cold radiance rises. Having eaten his fill, he sleeps soundly and contentedly;
he does not know that his body lies within the autumn waves.

When one who clears the paths through the marshy fields seeks to speak of the surging waves of the great ocean, the practitioner’s power of aspiration is firm; with a single stroke at the head, ten thousand acres are seen as level fields.
Guang, the *karmadāna*, returns to his native land;
light and environment both vanish. The cold pond is clear to its very bottom; tracing the current, a great wave overturns. The fifty-four prefectures are startled.
Sent to Master Chijue of Tiantong.
Decrepit in the Western Mountains, unable to do a hundred things; I rely on a single cane that accompanies me.
Propping it up here and there to pass idle days, I am content to be a monk in a small hermitage on a desolate mountain.
Master Da, you who seek words for the Way, must first subdue the six thieves. Once the six thieves are subdued, what is there to be gained? The ten directions are cut off;
the eye’s field is empty. Within Guanyin Monastery, there is no Maitreya.

Biyun Sends Greetings to an Old Friend at Huazang From deep within Biyun, I gaze upon the lakes and mountains; At times, I walk alone through the pine gateways. The old friends of my youth are nowhere to be seen;
I hear only the "guan-guan" calls of the secluded birds.
Seeing the attendant seeking words—three calls and three responses, like the point of an arrow meeting its target; when no longer called, there is no response, and the whole body is revealed.
From Xuedou to Ling Shan, you have trodden every step without deviation.
Master Guang requested these words:
"The radiant light shines silently and pervasively throughout the sands of the Ganges; yet if you cling to it, as before, your eyes will be filled with flowers.

When all conditions are exhausted and you turn your head to look, the four directions are vast and empty, utterly free from obstruction. Even this state of being free from obstruction is not yet the ultimate; you must further realize that there is the Patriarch."
The Master’s Barrier. Having penetrated this barrier, birth-and-death, Buddhas, and demons are all mere dung and urine. When the time comes, a clap of thunder resounds across the level ground;
the four seas and five lakes boil like a cauldron.

The matter of seeking words from an ancient Chan practitioner remains complete throughout all time. Why labor in vain to travel everywhere seeking it? Only when the straw sandals are worn through will one know the essential point;
then one regrets having traversed mountains and rivers, for the regret grows ever deeper.

The Buddha-work of the Elder Puxian has not yet emerged from his mother’s womb; this single phrase pervades heaven and earth, utterly free from error or deception. Without cause or reason, he suddenly sets out to act.
The feet: It is as if one were about to cast one’s body into a net. Suddenly, this blank net is severed; looking around, all is vast and empty, without boundaries or shores.
Amidst a mass of fierce flames, the wheel of Dharma is turned; the Buddhas of the three periods stand upon the ground and watch.
Whether the Venerable Miaokan enters the stupa or not,
whether it is auspicious or inauspicious— ultimately, in the end, it matters nothing. When the ashes fly and the smoke is extinguished,
a single sword leans against the cold heavens.
The Stele Inscription:

In Qi, within Zizhou, there is a magnificent place. There was a son of the Shui family who found no flavor in reading secular texts; he cherished the *palm-leaf* scriptures (Buddhist sutras) as if they were more delightful than beef or mutton.
His resolve to transcend the mundane world was so keen that his parents could not dissuade him by any means. He entered the Wencai Academy of Dangxian.

With the monk Puming as his teacher, he completed his full ordination (*upasampadā*). He then traveled to Dàshèngshàn Temple in Chengdu, where he selected eminent masters of the three studies (*tri-śikṣā*) to serve as his teachers, regarding them with the reverence due to a master.
Before long, he took up his staff and departed through the Three Gorges, proceeding directly to Huázàng Temple in Pílíng to pay his respects to Túdú Cè.
Cè recognized his potential and appointed him as an attendant at his side. When Cè later moved to Jìngshān, [Tàohé] accompanied him there. Cè—
Xǐ often entered the inner quarters. The Master went straight forward and said, "This is not the intention of the ancients. Whenever [Xǐ] presented a difficult point, the Master would not listen.
Dú'ān Yǎn, the First Seat in the hall, was his counterpart; thus he relied on Yǎn to resolve his doubts. When Yǎn opened the *Dharmapada-kośa*, he also accompanied him.
He took up the position at Qīngzhēn in Jīnlíng, where he offered the incense of gratitude for Yǎn’s guidance. Late in life...
He resided at Xiaolinyi on Mount Siming, maintaining his integrity with the austerity of ice and gall. Others could not endure his distress.

At the age of ninety, having observed seventy-three years of the monastic precepts, he passed away without illness on the nineteenth day of the second month in the second year of the Chunyou era. His remains were kept in the sarcophagus for seven days;
he was then buried in full body at the eastern corner of the temple. Having obtained an inscription that left him no cause for shame, the eulogy says: The eulogy says: [Insert eulogy here]
In the void, the sutra is preached; four flowers fall in profusion. Master Liang does not come, yet the voices of ten thousand apertures are silenced.
The Dharma would not have remained in stagnation had it not been for the sudden emergence of Ziliang. Liang was naturally reticent, yet through his reticence he championed the pure and true.
At Maozhu in Jinling, a place of exquisite beauty, he gave a brief demonstration of the total teaching, though the mist settled over half the fortress.
Taking the past as a mirror, using one’s own body as a substitute for a tongue, struggling and striving throughout life, I have finally attained complete realization at the small Lingyin Monastery.
Nearby is the small Jingci Monastery; I raise this banner of victory. My thoughts drift far away.
On the first day of spring in the third year of the Chunyou era, written by the resident monk of Jingci, Beijian (Jujian), on the west side of Lake Hu.
Dang. The Old Man of the Western Hills speaks as he has realized and acts as he has spoken; he does not indulge in artificial refinement, but is complete and natural as if formed by Heaven.
Every sentence strikes out the very marrow of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; every character opens the eyes of the monks. Yet, the patterns of his literary brilliance remain unmanifested.

At that time, it was offered; the perfect sound pierced the ears as if he were still alive. Written respectfully by the Tiantong bhikṣu (Dàochōng) on the Double Fifth of the second year of the Chūnyù era.
The old man Zhenru of West Mountain does not concern himself with branches and leaves; he possesses the refined air of an ancient master.

When later students examine this record, they will know that my words are not empty. Written with reverence on the night of the Lantern Festival in the year of Kaimao, Chunyou (1243), by Yuanzhao Srou (Shifan) of Mount Jing.
The *Kuyā Manroku*, Middle Volume, states: Zen Master Ryō of Seizan composed a verse on Zhaozhou’s interrogation of the old woman, which says:
"When hungry, one surely hears hunger; when full, one surely hears satiety. The old woman was at Mount Tiantai; Zhaozhou has thoroughly investigated her.
Dun’an Keyi, upon assuming the abbacy at Jingling Qingzhen, delivered his teachings with words that were as swift and precise as the trigger of a crossbow.
He wrote to Chijue at Tiantong, saying: "Decrepit as I am in the Western Hills, there is nothing I can carry with me except for a single cane, which leans east and west to pass my idle days.
I am content to be a monk in a small, secluded temple on a desolate mountain. He lived out his life at Xiaolingyin in Siming.
A native of Shu, the Western Hills, he was by nature upright and refined; he took no pleasure in associating with worldly folk. Wuzu—
His words are recorded as those of a master who remained true to his original nature.
Furthermore, the lower fascicle states: "Zen Master Liang of Xishan was a native of Fuzhou. He was austere and lived with great frugality;

he once possessed a single paper quilt that was nearly entirely patched and mended, yet he never changed it regardless of the cold or heat. From the Head Seat’s quarters at Gushan, he proceeded to Yun..."
When he was invited to serve as abbot at Men and later moved to Huangbo, he never once changed his bedding. One night, an attendant monk secretly replaced it with a silk quilt.
Yuanliang cried out in alarm and rebuked him, saying, "I have little merit; throughout my life, I have never dared to wear silk.
Moreover, this blanket has accompanied me for thirty years—how could it be discarded? Those who heard this remarked that his dwelling on the mountain possessed an air of antiquity.
Ren Renfeng subsequently left his seat and entered the mountains of Yongyang and Yanhu. There, he lived as a practitioner who tilled the soil with a knife and sowed by fire;
nothing was known of his final end. (According to the Japanese scholar Dōchū, this Xishan [West Mountain] is not the one associated with Sifu Dun’an.)
